title: Concentration Inequalities and Martingale Inequalities: A Survey
abstractRaw: We examine a number of generalized and extended versions of concentration inequalities and martingale inequalities. These inequalities are effective for analyzing processes with quite general conditions as illustrated in an example for an infinite Polya process and web graphs.

title: Psychometric Validation of a Deep Learning-based Foreground Speech Detection Algorithm for Everyday Conversation Detection
authors: Amanda M. Bernal, Johannes Leonhard Klinz, Valeria Pfeifer, David Sbarra, Charles L Raison, Nicole Nugent, Rajat Hebbar, Shrikanth Narayanan, Matthias R Mehl
abstractRaw: Passive ambient audio sampling bears great potential for objectively measuring daily social activity and its association with wellbeing and health. However, detecting true conversations via human annotation is labor-intensive, and automatic labeling via audio signal processing has thus far only received proof-of-concept validation. Here, we conduct a comprehensive psychometric validation of a deep learning-based foreground speech detection algorithm for conversation activity detection (CAD) from ambient audio sampled with the Electronically Activated Recorder (EAR) method (Hebbar et al., 2021). We assess the CAD algorithm’s validity as an objective measure of conversation activity using four archival EAR datasets with human ground-truth conversation annotations (N = 566 participants, n = 167,539 audio recordings). Specifically, we evaluate, across the four samples, the degree to which the CAD algorithm converges with human-annotated conversation activity, yields temporal stability estimates of conversation activity, and replicates patterns of external correlates (with demographic, wellbeing, and personality measures) comparable to those derived from human ground-truth annotations. We further compare the distributional properties of conversation activity derived from the CAD algorithm and human ground-truth annotations and use this information for thresholding the algorithm’s continuous conversation activity estimates. Overall, the CAD algorithm evidences strong psychometric properties for estimating conversation activity across a range of participants and study characteristics, suggesting that it is suitable for at-scale deployment to objectively measure daily socializing from passively sampled ambient audio.

title: Replicating patterns of Issue Alignment and Issue Asymmetry
authors: Bart de Bruin, Yijing Chen, Philip Warncke, Dino Carpentras
abstractRaw: Classic opinion dynamics models typically focus on a single opinion or treat them as independent dimensions. Several empirical studies indicate however that attitudes are interdependent and embedded within structured belief systems. These systems exhibit a mix of order and variability that standard opinion dynamics models cannot capture. In this work, we have developed an agent-based model that integrates cognitive consistency pressure with attitude structures to recreate these patterns. Specifically, we test two mechanisms through which agents perceive consistency among opinions: one grounded in issue-level associations, and another based on co-occurrence patterns at the position level. Our simulations show that neither mechanism alone is sufficient to reproduce the empirical complexity of empirical belief systems. However, a hybrid approach combining both mechanisms generates attitude structures that closely resemble empirical data. Our findings highlight the role of social perception in shaping belief systems and suggest a novel modelling pathway for studying ideological polarisation across multiple issue domains.

title: Business-size bias in consumer dishonesty: People are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones
authors: Jareef Martuza, Hallgeir Sjåstad, Helge Thorbjørnsen
abstractRaw: Consumer dishonest behavior—such as insurance fraud and retail theft—costs businesses billions of dollars every year. Are some businesses more likely to be cheated than others? While classic philosophical perspectives contend that moral transgressions—like dishonesty—are equally wrong regardless of the victim, we suggest that people perceive small organizations as more victim-like than big organizations, which increases the moral cost of cheating small organizations. Supporting this hypothesis, six main and eight supplemental studies (N = 10,436) reveal that people are less likely to cheat small businesses than big ones, a robust effect across both scenario-based and incentive-compatible experiments. Further, people perceive small businesses as more vulnerable and moral than big businesses, which mediates lower dishonesty toward small businesses. Finally, enhancing big business’ vulnerability and morality can reduce dishonesty toward them. Thus, beyond financial incentives and internal moral standards, dishonest behavior is also shaped by characteristics of the victim.

title: Flavour through the lens of conflict
authors: Alice Albertini Drew, Massimiliano Zampini, Salvador Soto-Faraco
abstractRaw: For many, flavour is the quintessential multisensory experience. It emerges from synthesizing information across sensory modalities and temporal scales. Disparities between these cues are inevitable, and regulation is necessary to synthesize a unitary flavour percept, triggering hedonic and attentional responses, and ultimately liking. Although several frameworks address specific consequences of flavour incongruity, an integrative account unifying perceptual, attentional, hedonic, and adaptive responses remains poorly specified. Here, we explore whether the principles of conflict monitoring, originally developed to explain sensorimotor competition, can be extended to explain the dynamics of competition between flavour-related perceptual representations. We argue that brain mechanisms that monitor for, signal, and regulate discrepancies in information processing can help explain how incongruent flavour cues are resolved, how attention and hedonic responses are modulated, and how flavour representations are updated through experience. This framework is complementary with existing accounts based on predictive processing, causal inference, associative learning, and assimilation–contrast, by specifying when unresolved competition between flavour representations recruits attentional control and adaptive learning. Considering the role of conflict mechanisms in flavour can provide some unification across existing accounts and suggest avenues for research both in the laboratory as well as in the consumer industry.

title: Fifty Shades of Well-Being: Addressing an Overlooked Source of Confusion in the Science of Well-Being.
abstractRaw: Despite constant progress, the science of well-being remains marked by confusion, with a proliferation of competing conceptual frameworks, theoretical approaches, and measurement tools undermining both scientific progress and real-world applications in areas such as counseling, therapy, and public policy. This paper identifies an overlooked contributor to this confusion: the adoption of Philosophically Dense Concepts (PDC) into empirical science, facilitated by academic practices that favor theoretical novelty and discourage interdisciplinary collaboration. Using a conceptual genealogy of the hedonic-eudaimonic well-being distinction as a paradigmatic example, I show how such PDC, when translated from philosophy into psychology and social and health sciences, became semantically fuzzy and led to inconsistent theoretical frameworks and measurement tools. The paper concludes with recommendations on how to better deal with PDC in well-being research and the emerging science of flourishing.
